title: Working with time series data
notes: Scope is Part 1 only: ts/zoo/xts/tsibble objects, the index, plotting, EDA, calendar effects, missing values. All output blocks verified against local R 4.6.0.

questions.prompt: You have a numeric vector of 120 monthly sales figures in chronological order. Why is wrapping it in a time series object worth the trouble, rather than just working with the vector?

options.text: The object stores the time index alongside the values, so functions know the sampling frequency and where each observation falls in the calendar.
Time series objects are stored more compactly in memory than plain numeric vectors.
A vector cannot hold more than 100 observations without losing precision.
Arithmetic on a time series object is faster because it is written in C.

questions.why: A ts, zoo, xts or tsibble carries the index. That is what lets seasonal plots, lag operations and forecast functions know what a period means.

questions.prompt: A monthly series is created starting in April 2023 with twelve observations. What do these three results tell you about where the series ends?

options.text: The series runs April 2023 to March 2024, because twelve monthly observations from April 2023 land on March of the next year.
The series runs April 2023 to April 2024, because the start month repeats at the end of a full year.
The series runs April 2023 to December 2023, and the 2024 in end() is the year the object was created.
The end value is wrong; ts objects always end in December of the starting year.

questions.why: end() reports year 2024, period 3. With frequency 12, period 3 is March. Twelve observations beginning in month 4 finish in month 3 of the following year.

questions.prompt: This quarterly series holds the integers 1 to 24 beginning in Q1 2020. Why does the window shown contain 6, 7 and 8?
questions.code:
y <- ts(1:24, start = c(2020, 1), frequency = 4)
window(y, start = c(2021, 2), end = c(2021, 4))
#>      Qtr2 Qtr3 Qtr4
#> 2021    6    7    8

options.text: Because 2020 uses observations 1 to 4, so Q2 2021 is the sixth observation, and window() selects by calendar position rather than by row number.
Because window() always drops the first year of any series before selecting.
Because window() counts backwards from the end of the series.
Because the values were re-indexed when the ts object was created.

questions.why: Q1 to Q4 of 2020 are observations 1 to 4, so Q1 2021 is the fifth and Q2 2021 the sixth. window() speaks in calendar time, not row positions.

questions.prompt: Your data arrives with irregular timestamps: several readings some days, none on others. Which object handles this most naturally?

options.text: xts or zoo, because both store an arbitrary ordered index rather than assuming a fixed frequency.
ts, because you can set frequency to the average number of readings per day.
ts, after rounding all timestamps to the nearest whole day.
None of these; irregular data cannot be represented as a time series in R.

questions.why: ts assumes evenly spaced observations and encodes time as a start plus a frequency. zoo and xts store the actual index, so irregular spacing is not a problem.

questions.prompt: What does the key of a tsibble specify?

options.text: The columns that identify separate series within the table.
The column holding the timestamps, which orders the rows.
The variable you intend to forecast from the others.
The spacing between consecutive observations in time.

questions.why: The index is time, the key is identity. Together they must be unique, which is exactly the constraint that lets a tsibble hold many series at once.

questions.prompt: as_tsibble() rejects your data frame with a message about duplicate rows. What has almost certainly happened?

options.text: The combination of index and key appears more than once, usually because a grouping column was left out of the key.
The data frame contains missing values in the measured column.
The timestamps are not sorted in ascending order.
The data frame has more rows than tsibble allows.

questions.why: Two rows sharing a timestamp are only duplicates if nothing distinguishes them. Naming the distinguishing column as part of the key resolves it.

questions.prompt: A daily tsibble covers a year but has only 350 rows. What is the practical consequence of leaving those gaps implicit?

options.text: Lag-based operations treat the row before as the previous period even when days are missing, so lags and rolling windows silently span the gaps.
The tsibble refuses to print until the gaps are filled.
Nothing; a tsibble stores its own calendar and compensates automatically.
The series is automatically converted to weekly frequency.

questions.why: An implicit gap is invisible to row-based operations. Making gaps explicit is what stops a lag from quietly reaching across a missing week.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about a time plot are true?

options.text: It reveals structure such as trend, level shifts and outliers that a summary table cannot show.
It shows the order of observations, which is the information a histogram throws away.
It is only informative once the series has been made stationary.
It requires at least two full seasonal cycles before it can be drawn.

questions.why: The whole point of a time plot is that it preserves order. A histogram of the same numbers discards exactly the information that matters.

questions.prompt: A seasonal plot draws each year as its own line against the month on the horizontal axis. What does this show that an ordinary time plot does not?

options.text: Whether the same months are consistently high or low, and whether that pattern is changing from year to year.
The overall direction of the trend across the whole sample.
Whether the residuals are normally distributed.
The precise numerical value of the seasonal component.

questions.why: Stacking years on a common seasonal axis makes the shape of the season directly comparable, and makes a change in that shape visible.

questions.prompt: The seasonal swings in a series get visibly wider as the level rises. What does that pattern suggest?

options.text: The seasonality is multiplicative, so a log or Box-Cox transform will make the variation roughly constant.
The series contains outliers that should be deleted before modelling.
The series is stationary and needs no further treatment.
The seasonal period has been misidentified and should be doubled.

questions.why: Swings proportional to the level are the signature of multiplicative seasonality. A variance-stabilising transform turns it into an additive problem.

questions.prompt: A lag plot of a monthly series shows a tight positive band at lag 12 but a diffuse cloud at lag 1. What does that combination say?

options.text: The series is driven by an annual seasonal pattern rather than by short-run month-to-month momentum.
The series has a strong upward trend and no seasonality.
The series is white noise at every lag.
The series has been differenced twice already.

questions.why: Structure at lag 12 with little at lag 1 means this month resembles the same month last year far more than it resembles last month.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes exploratory analysis of a time series from exploratory analysis of ordinary cross-sectional data?

options.text: Order carries information, so observations are not exchangeable and the usual independence assumptions do not hold.
Time series data cannot contain missing values.
Time series always require larger samples before any summary is meaningful.
Correlation cannot be computed on time series data.

questions.why: Shuffling rows destroys a time series but leaves a cross-section intact. Every difference in method follows from that one fact.

questions.prompt: In a classical decomposition of a monthly series, what is the remainder?

options.text: What is left once trend and season are removed, which should look like noise.
The forecast error measured on a held-out test set.
The difference between the first and the last observation.
The portion of the series that failed to parse on import.

questions.why: Trend plus season plus remainder reconstructs the series. Structure remaining in the remainder is a sign the decomposition missed something.

questions.prompt: An ACF plot of monthly data shows bars that decay slowly and stay well outside the confidence bounds for twenty lags. What does this indicate?

options.text: A trend, because a trending series stays close to its recent values so autocorrelation dies away slowly.
Pure white noise, because the bars form a smooth pattern.
Strong seasonality with no trend, because seasonality always produces slow decay.
A calculation error, because the ACF cannot exceed the bounds at more than one lag.

questions.why: Slow decay across many lags is the classic trend signature. Seasonality shows as spikes at multiples of the period, not as uniform slow decay.

questions.prompt: You want to check whether the remainder from a decomposition is effectively noise. What is the appropriate check?

options.text: Look at the ACF of the remainder for bars outside the bounds, and confirm with a portmanteau test such as Ljung-Box.
Confirm that the remainder has a mean of exactly zero.
Check that the remainder has the same variance as the original series.
Verify that the remainder contains no negative values.

questions.why: Noise means no remaining autocorrelation. The ACF shows it by eye, and Ljung-Box tests the whole set of lags at once.

questions.prompt: Monthly retail revenue is compared across months without adjustment. Why does this mislead even when nothing about the business has changed?

options.text: Months contain different numbers of days and different numbers of trading days, so the totals differ for calendar reasons alone.
Revenue is always recorded with a one-month lag.
Monthly data cannot be compared without first taking logarithms.
Seasonal effects cancel out over any twelve-month window, so comparison is meaningless.

questions.why: February has 28 days and March 31. A calendar adjustment removes the part of the difference that is arithmetic rather than commercial.

questions.prompt: Why do seven separate day-of-week counts often work better as predictors than a single trading-day total?

options.text: Because different weekdays carry different volumes, and a single total forces them all to share one coefficient.
Because a single total cannot be computed reliably in R.
Because seven predictors always fit better than one, whatever the data.
Because the total ignores public holidays, which the seven counts include automatically.

questions.why: A Saturday and a Tuesday are not worth the same. Separate counts let the model learn each day's contribution instead of averaging them.

questions.prompt: An hourly series recorded in a zone that observes daylight saving contains a day with 23 hourly rows and another with 25. What is happening?

options.text: The clock change removes one local hour in spring and repeats one in autumn, so local days genuinely differ in length.
The logging system dropped and duplicated rows at random.
The timestamps were parsed with the wrong format string.
The series was aggregated from a finer frequency incorrectly.

questions.why: Local time is not uniform across a DST boundary. Working in UTC and converting for display avoids the missing and duplicated hours.

questions.prompt: A colleague fills every gap in a seasonal series with the overall series mean. What does this do to the analysis?

options.text: It flattens the seasonal pattern at the filled points and shrinks the apparent variance, biasing anything estimated afterwards.
It is the safest choice because the mean is unbiased by construction.
It has no effect provided fewer than ten percent of values are missing.
It inflates the variance and makes confidence intervals too wide.

questions.why: A mean fill ignores both level and season. Every filled point is pulled to the middle, which flattens structure and understates variability.
questions.chapter_title: Missing values in time series in R

questions.prompt: Linear interpolation is applied to a vector with three missing values. Why are the two consecutive gaps filled with 8 and 10?
questions.code:
z <- c(4, NA, 6, NA, NA, 12)
zoo::na.approx(z, na.rm = FALSE)
#> [1]  4  5  6  8 10 12

options.text: Interpolation draws a straight line between the known values 6 and 12, so the two gaps take the evenly spaced points along it.
Each gap is filled with the value immediately before it, then rounded upward.
The gaps take the mean of all observed values in the vector.
The gaps are filled by repeating the first interpolated value, 5.

questions.why: Between 6 and 12 there are three equal steps of 2, giving 8 and 10. The single earlier gap between 4 and 6 gets the midpoint, 5.
questions.chapter_title: Missing values in time series in R

questions.prompt: A strongly seasonal monthly series has a three-month gap. Why is plain linear interpolation a poor choice here?

options.text: It draws a straight line through what should be a seasonal swing, erasing the pattern exactly where the data is already weakest.
It cannot be computed when more than one consecutive value is missing.
It always produces values outside the observed range.
It requires the series to be stationary first.

questions.why: Interpolation assumes the series moves smoothly between endpoints. A seasonal series does not, so the fill flattens the season it should reproduce.
questions.chapter_title: Missing values in time series in R

questions.prompt: What is the honest way to decide which imputation method suits a particular series?

options.text: Remove known values at random to create artificial gaps, fill them with each method, and compare against the values you held back.
Choose whichever method produces the smoothest looking filled series.
Choose whichever method changes the series mean least.
Always prefer the most sophisticated method available.

questions.why: You cannot score a fill against values you never had. Deleting known points creates ground truth and turns the choice into a measurement.
questions.chapter_title: Missing values in time series in R

questions.prompt: Which two are genuine advantages of a tsibble over a ts object?

options.text: It can hold many series at once, distinguished by a key.
It keeps the timestamps as a real column, so ordinary data-frame verbs work on it.
It automatically removes outliers when the object is created.
It computes forecasts without a model being specified.

questions.why: A ts holds one series and hides time inside attributes. A tsibble holds many, keeps time visible, and stays compatible with the tidyverse.

questions.prompt: cycle() is applied to a short monthly series beginning in November 2022. What is it reporting?
questions.code:
cycle(ts(1:6, start = c(2022, 11), frequency = 12))
#>      Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec
#> 2022                                          11  12
#> 2023   1   2   3   4

options.text: The position of each observation within its seasonal cycle, so November is 11 and the series rolls over to 1 in January.
The values stored in the series, rearranged into calendar order.
The number of observations recorded in each month.
The number of months since the series began.

questions.why: cycle() returns the seasonal position, not the data. That is what makes it useful for building month dummies or grouping by season.

questions.prompt: A daily series of website visits shows a repeating seven-day shape. In tsibble terms, what should the interval be?

options.text: One day, because the interval describes how often observations are recorded, not the length of the repeating pattern.
One week, because the pattern repeats weekly.
Seven days divided by the number of series in the key.
It should be left unset so tsibble can infer it during modelling.

questions.why: Interval is the spacing of the data. The seasonal period is a separate idea, and confusing the two is a common source of broken models.

questions.prompt: Why is a subseries plot, which draws each month in its own small panel with that month's mean marked, worth drawing after a seasonal plot?

options.text: Whether an individual month is drifting over the years, which overlap can hide.
The overall level of the series across the whole sample period.
Whether the residuals still carry autocorrelation at short lags.
The forecast distribution expected for each month ahead.

questions.why: A seasonal plot answers which months are high. A subseries plot answers whether a given month is drifting, which is a different question.

questions.prompt: Before modelling, you find that the gaps in your daily series fall almost entirely on public holidays. Why does that matter more than the number of gaps?

options.text: The missingness is systematic rather than random, so any fill that ignores the holiday effect will bias those days in a predictable direction.
Holidays cannot be represented in a tsibble index.
Systematic gaps are always safe to drop entirely.
It does not matter, because imputation methods correct for it automatically.

questions.why: Randomly scattered gaps and systematically placed gaps call for different treatment. Knowing why a value is missing is part of deciding how to fill it.
questions.chapter_title: Missing values in time series in R

questions.prompt: You convert a monthly ts object into a tsibble to use tidyverse verbs. What must be true for the result to be a valid tsibble?

options.text: Each row must be uniquely identified by its index, plus a key if the data holds more than one series.
The measured column must contain no missing values.
The index must be a Date rather than a year-month type.
The series must contain at least two full seasonal cycles.

questions.why: Uniqueness of index plus key is the one hard constraint. Everything else about a tsibble is convenience built on top of it.

questions.prompt: Which two checks belong in the first pass of exploratory analysis on a new series?

options.text: Plot the series against time and look for trend, seasonality, level shifts and outliers.
Check whether the index is regular and whether any periods are missing.
Fit an ARIMA model and inspect its coefficients.
Compute the forecast accuracy on a holdout sample.

questions.why: Look at it, and check the calendar underneath it. Fitting and scoring models come later, and both depend on these two being sound.

questions.prompt: A monthly series of total sales rises steadily. A colleague concludes the business is growing. What adjustment would you check first?

options.text: Whether the rise survives dividing by population or customer count.
Whether the rows were sorted correctly by date on import.
Whether the seasonal period should be 12 rather than 4.
Whether the values are stored as numeric rather than integer.

questions.why: Totals confound size with intensity. Dividing by the relevant base separates growth in the business from growth in the denominator.
